body: Economists call this the lipstick effect.
Tight budgets can push bigger luxuries aside.
A lipstick may still feel like affordable comfort.
Juliet Schor described this behavior in 1998.
Leonard Lauder popularized the lipstick index in 2001.
He linked stronger lipstick sales with economic weakness.
The idea became a quirky recession signal.
But later downturns did not reliably repeat it.
So lipstick is not a dependable economic indicator.
And lipstick syndrome is not a recognized medical diagnosis.
optional_closing: The supposed syndrome is really a nickname for small comfort under pressure.
full_narration: When market money runs short, why does one tiny luxury survive? Here's the reason. That contradiction sends me reaching for the answer. Economists call this the lipstick effect. Tight budgets can push bigger luxuries aside. A lipstick may still feel like affordable comfort. Juliet Schor described this behavior in 1998. Leonard Lauder popularized the lipstick index in 2001. He linked stronger lipstick sales with economic weakness. The idea became a quirky recession signal. But later downturns did not reliably repeat it. So lipstick is not a dependable economic indicator. And lipstick syndrome is not a recognized medical diagnosis. The supposed syndrome is really a nickname for small comfort under pressure.
